title: Add `struct r_dict` to the rlang C library
description:
- `r_dict_put()` takes a key and a value. It returns `true` if `key` has been added to the dict or `false` if the key already exists.

- Keys are hashed with `XXH3_64bits()`. It is exposed as a C callable and made available in the rlang lib.

- Keys are compared by pointer. We could add `r_dict_set_cmp()` to set a comparison function later on. Pointer comparison of keys is useful for collecting objects by reference. It also works with SYMSXP or CHARSXP since those are interned.

- The hash table is implemented like R environments (list of pairlist buckets). It is rounded up to the nearest power of 2 to help with collisions. It grows by 2 when the load factor reaches 0.75.

- Protection is handled with a `shelter` element. Callers only need to protect this shelter which is updated in place during resizes.

title: Use `memcpy()` to copy over the native encoding size
description:
Hopefully fixes this gcc11 warning:
https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/bdr/gcc11/rlang.out

I think the problem comes with casting the `void*` to a `int*` to extract out the `int` representing the native encoding size that we know is there. The `void*` is probably really a `unsigned char*` under the hood, and gcc11 is probably picking up that it looks like we are trying to extract an `int` from an `unsigned char*`?

The fix here copies what R does in `R_Unserialize()` to get at that native encoding size. They use a `memcpy()` in `InBytes()` to just copy over the bytes directly into an `int`.
https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/d22ee2fc0dc8142b23eed9f46edf76ea9d3ca69a/src/main/serialize.c#L421
https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/d22ee2fc0dc8142b23eed9f46edf76ea9d3ca69a/src/main/serialize.c#L2767

title: Add POC simple hashing function with MD5 backend
description:
This PR adds a POC for `hash()` - a hashing function for arbitrary R objects backed by MD5.

It uses an implementation of MD5 placed in the open domain with absolutely no warranty or copyright.
https://openwall.info/wiki/people/solar/software/public-domain-source-code/md5

Supposedly this impl is used in PHP and Freetype, so I feel pretty good about it.

It passes the small test suite proposed in this RFC standard for MD5. Note that they also provide an implementation, which I tried using first, but it assumed a 32 bit system and was returning incorrect results. The implementation used here explicitly states that it overcomes those limitations.
https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc1321

I've kept the copied files in `src/internal/md5/`. Then `hash.c` includes the `md5.c` file at the top. This seemed reasonable based on how you include other `.c` files (like in the top level `internal.c`), but let me know if you'd like it set up differently.

---

I have absolutely no idea what the "best" arguments to `serialize()` are, but `version = 2` seems reasonable to be reproducible on older versions of R.

The `hash_string()` function is mainly for testing.

Closes #1031

The original inclusion was inspired by code in readxl and readr that controls progress. However, in that case, the motivation is about performance, not about lack of interactivity *per se*.

title: Issue924: Resolve Normal Tilde's in Quosures
description:
Fix #924 

This ended up a bit complicated as in order to work correctly we have to search through all the enclosures while also skipping the mask environment, so we couldn't just rely on `Rf_findFun`.  I'm also not a huge fan of how the KEEP/FREE business ended up in `findTilde`, but I didn't want to resort to more complex PROTECT stack management (that I'm less familiar with).

Note this does not correctly resolve things like `get('~')` which will return the Rlang tilde.  I tested this with valgrind, SAN, and rchk.  For rchk, there are errors, but they appear to be from code I did not touch:

title: Review display of chained errors
description:
* We now climb the ancestry of chained errors to find the oldest parent errors carrying a backtrace and display this backtrace in full. This is the oldest and thus most complete backtrace.

* We no longer decompose backtraces across error contexts because there is no way for us to do this with calling handlers. Calling handlers are now the preferred methods of rethrowing errors because they preserve the stack and allow users to `recover()` the error.

* The combination of these two changes produces consistent error and backtrace output for errors rethrown from both `tryCatch()` and `withCallingHandlers()`.

* The error ancestry is reflected with a tree display for error messages. The first message for the youngest error (highest level) is generated with `conditionMessage()`. The messages for older errors are generated with `cnd_header()`. This avoids repetition when the younger errors reuse parts of the messages of their parent errors, e.g. in bullets.

Closes #851

title: Implement `set_names()` in C
description:
To do this, I've had to implement a few other things in C:

- `is_function()`

   - While I was there, I went ahead and did `is_closure()`, `is_primitive()`, `is_primitive_eager()` and `is_primitive_lazy()` too

- `is_formula()`

- `names2()`

I've created a new file, `internal/attr.c` to house the C implementations of `set_names()` and `names2()`.

For `names2()`, we fall back to the R level `names()` when `x` is an object to allow it to dispatch. We also handle pairlists and language objects specially, like `getAttrib()` does.

For `set_names()`, we always eventually set the names with `names<-()` rather than with `r_poke_names()`. The reason for this is that `do_namesgets()` has the ability to shallow copy _attributes_ using an ALTREP wrapper with `R_shallow_duplicate_attr()`. This isn't exposed to us yet from C, but calling `names<-` and getting a wrapper object is way faster than calling `r_maybe_duplicate()`, which will duplicate `x`.

I have allowed the new `r_as_function()` to call out to `rlang::as_function()` for simplicity. I have seen that you worked on a partial implementation of a C `as_function()` in vctrs, but the quosure handling here looks tricky to me. Feel free to take over and implement that if you want 😬

title: Add `check_downstream_deps()`
description:
Branched from #926. Implemented in a standalone compat file that can be copied in zero-dep packages, but will eventually be exported from rlang as well.

Sometimes a package is updated with known breaking changes. Broken downstream dependencies can then be updated to fix the breakage and bump the required version of the upstream package in their DESCRIPTION file. However that doesn't cover the common case of updating the upstream dependencies independently. Since there is no way of specifying minimal versions of downstream dependencies in DESCRIPTION, the downstream packages won't be updated even though they are no longer compatible. This can result in surprising and hard to debug behaviour.

The goal of `check_downstream_deps()` is to reduce friction when breaking updates are released with known downstream dependencies requirements. One instance where these requirements are known ahead of time is when the maintainer owns both the upstream and downstream packages and coordinates a joint release to CRAN.

`check_downstream_deps()` takes named vectors of `min` and `from` components. `min` is the minimum version of the downstream package that is compatible with the upstream package. `from` is the earliest version of the upstream package that is compatible with that minimum version. For instance here is the downstream-deps spec for rlang:

```r
.onLoad <- function(lib, pkg) {
  check_downstream_deps(
    pkg,
    dplyr = c(min = "0.8.0", from = "0.4.0")
  )
}
```

If the user has updated rlang but not dplyr, they get this warning once the load is complete:

```r
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))
#> Warning message:
#> As of rlang 0.4.0, dplyr must be at least version 0.8.0.
#> ✖ dplyr 0.7.2 is too old for rlang 0.4.4.
#> ℹ Please update dplyr with `install.packages("dplyr")` and restart R.
```

As in #926, Windows users receive specific advice about safe installation on that platform:

```r
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))
#> Warning message:
#> As of rlang 0.4.0, dplyr must be at least version 0.8.0.
#> ✖ dplyr 0.7.2 is too old for rlang 0.4.4.
#> ℹ Please update dplyr to the latest version.
#> ℹ Updating packages on Windows requires precautions:
#>   <https://github.com/jennybc/what-they-forgot/issues/62>
```

title: Add `check_linked_version()`
description:
Implements `check_linked_version()` in a standalone file that can be copied in zero-dep packages. After some testing in other packages it will be exported from rlang as well.

Packages that include native code are fragile on Windows and might not be properly updated. When the package is loaded in memory, R might install a new version of the package without updating the corresponding DLL because. With `check_linked_version()` you can preventively inform your users about broken installation.

It should be called from the `.onLoad()` hook:

```r
.onLoad <- function(lib, pkg) {
  check_linked_version(pkg, with_rlang = FALSE)
}
```

It expects that the namespace of the checked package contains a C callable called `*pkgname*_linked_version()`. This callable should return the package version as a string. The version recorded in the native library is then compared to the one returned from `packageVersion()`. If they don't match, an informative error is thrown:

```r
Error: The vctrs package is not properly installed.
✖ The DLL version (0.10.99.9005) does not correspond to the package version (0.2.99.9005).
ℹ Please update vctrs with `install.packages("vctrs")` and restart R.
```

On Windows the error message includes additional advice from jennybc/what-they-forgot#62 about safely reinstalling packages:

```r
Error: The vctrs package is not properly installed.
✖ The DLL version (0.10.99.9005) does not correspond to the package version (0.2.99.9005).
ℹ Please update vctrs to the latest version.
ℹ Updating packages on Windows requires precautions:
  <https://github.com/jennybc/what-they-forgot/issues/62>
```

~~A usethis tool will eventually make it easy to generate an up-to-date `version.c` file at each version bump.~~

title: Warn on load when downstream dep is incompatible
description:
A user mentioned a forward compatibility issue between rlang 0.4.0 and dplyr 0.7.8: https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/4600.

As I'm about to release rlang 0.4.1, I'd like to experiment with a load-time warning to detect packages known to be forward-incompatible. Loading rlang with an old dplyr would give this warning:

```
Warning message:
As of rlang 0.4.0, dplyr must be at least version 0.8.0.
✖ dplyr 0.7.8 is too old for rlang 0.4.1.
ℹ Please update dplyr with `install.packages("dplyr")`.
```

On Windows platforms, we link to https://github.com/jennybc/what-they-forgot/issues/62 where the second comment provide a rough guide on proper updating of packages.

```
Warning message:
As of rlang 0.4.0, dplyr must be at least version 0.8.0.
✖ dplyr 0.7.8 is too old for rlang 0.4.1.
ℹ Please update dplyr to the latest version.
ℹ Updating packages on Windows requires precautions:
  <https://github.com/jennybc/what-they-forgot/issues/62>.
```

title: Add `cnd_message()`, `cnd_issue()`, and `cnd_bullets()`
description:
`cnd_message()` is a function that assembles an error message from two generics, `cnd_issue()` and `cnd_bullets()`. Methods for `cnd_issue()` should return a single line. Methods for `cnd_bullets()` should return a character vector of lines.

The bullets are prefixed with `*`, `x`, or `i` depending on the names of the character vector.

- Elements named `"i"` are prefixed with a blue "info" symbol.
- Elements named `"x"` are prefixed with a red "cross" symbol.
- Unnamed elements are prefixed with a "*" symbol.

`cnd_message()` is called automatically by the `rlang_error` method for `conditionMessage()`, so that error classes only need to implement these two methods. The default methods are equivalent to just plucking `cnd$message`, so they can be left unimplemented as well.

If the error object contains a `.bullets` field containing a function, that method is called instead. This makes it possible to write very precise methods for generating the error bullets without having to overspecify the class hierarchy.

title: Simplify branch backtraces further
description:
This increases the simplification of branch backtraces by keeping track of lexical contexts of local closures. If a call frame A is hosted by a closure that was created on the stack at frame B, the latter frame is treated as the parent of A.

The main effect of this change is to merge all frames implicated in the invokation of the local closure, as well as the frame of the closure itself. It's as if the code was run from the function that created the closure:

```r
f <- function() lapply(NA, function(x) trace_back())
trace <- f()[[1]]

trace
#>     █
#>  1. └─global::f()
#>  2.   └─base::lapply(NA, function(x) trace_back())
#>  3.     └─FUN(X[[i]], ...)

print(trace, simplify = "branch")
#>  1. global::f()

```

This behaviour is recursive:

```r
f <- function() lapply(NA, function(x) lapply(NA, function(y) trace_back()))
trace <- f()[[1]][[1]]

trace
#>     █
#>  1. └─global::f()
#>  2.   └─base::lapply(NA, function(x) lapply(NA, function(y) trace_back()))
#>  3.     └─FUN(X[[i]], ...)
#>  4.       └─base::lapply(NA, function(y) trace_back())
#>  5.         └─FUN(X[[i]], ...)

print(trace, simplify = "branch")
#>  1. global::f()
```

This also applies to named local closures:

```r
f <- function() {
  g <- function(x) {
    h <- function(y) trace_back()
    h()
  }
  g()
}
trace <- f()

trace
#>     █
#>  1. └─global::f()
#>  2.   └─g()
#>  3.     └─h()

print(trace, simplify = "branch")
#>  1. global::f()
```

I think ideally we'd preserve the call frames of named closures, however R does not allow distinguishing between named and anonymous functions.

This automatically simplifies magrittr backtraces in a range of cases, though not all of them. I have removed the complex, difficult to maintain and buggy unrolling code in favour a simpler frame trimming to take care of the remaining cases of complex magrittr backtraces. This way we can experiment with terser backtraces, and if unrolling turns out better we could tackle it as part of tidyverse/magrittr#175.

title: Stop formatting rlang errors from `conditionMessage()` method
description:
This changes the strategy for formatting rlang errors and saving unhandled errors to `rlang::last_error()`. Currently all the logic is in the `conditionMessage()` method for rlang errors. This has several drawbacks:

* It is harder to implement a condition-message method for subclasses of rlang-error.

* Some functions like `try()` invoke the condition-message method, which causes backtraces (or reminders to call `last_error()`) to leak unexpectedly.

This PR moves the logic inside `abort()` with a new strategy, thanks to an idea from @gaborcsardi:

* To detect unhandled errors, we first `signalCondition()` the error object. If the error is handled this will cause a jump out of `abort()`. This can be overridden by setting the `rlang_force_unhandled_error` global option to `TRUE` (useful for unit tests).

* If we're still in `abort()` after signalling the condition, we save the error and format the message.

* To avoid logging errors multiple times from calling handlers, we `stop()` with a bare condition object that inherit only from `"condition"`.

title: Allow %|% to work when y is of same length as x
description:
These changes allow `x %|% y` when `y` is of same length as `x`. For example:
```r
> c(1L, NA, 3L, NA, NA) %|% 0L # usual use case
[1] 1 0 3 0 0
> c(1L, NA, 3L, NA, NA) %|% (6L:10L) # modified use case
[1]  1  7  3  9 10
```

Changes: 
 * `R/operators.R`: I modified the documentation of %|% to reflect the changes in behaviour of this function. I also modified the `stopifnot()` checks accordingly.
 * `src/lib/replace-na.c`: Rather than looking at the length of `y` in `replace_na_()`, I created a separate function `replace_na_vec_()` and call the correct function depending on the length of `y`, as not to sacrifice speed by having more if/else statements.
 * `tests/testthat/test-operators.R`: I added tests to check whether `x %|% y` is working correctly when `length(y) == length(x)`, and also that it produces an error when it is not.

title: Add `r_on_exit_callback()`
description:
`rlang_on_exit_callback` is an exported C callable that pushes an `on_exit()` event in the current call frame (typically the `.Call()` wrapper) to call back a C function with data.

The C library exposes it as `r_on_exit_callback()`.

It could be renamed to `r_on_exit()` if we find a better name for the version that takes R code to evaluate. In general it seems simpler to pass a C callback because you don't need to worry about scoping of the R code then, so the callback variant might end up more useful.

title: Add pairlist2()
description:
* New `pairlist2()` function to create pairlists with splicing support. It's mainly meant to support `call2()` but may also be useful for `new_function()`. It preserves empty arguments since those are useful in calls and formals lists.

* `call2()` is reimplemented in C and uses `pairlist2()` for capturing dots. This brings its performance closer to that of `base::call()`:

  ```r
  bench::mark(
    base = call("fn"),
    before = call2_before("fn"),
    after = call2("fn")
  )
  #>   expression     min    mean  median    max `itr/sec` mem_alloc  n_gc n_itr
  #>   <bch:expr> <bch:t> <bch:t> <bch:t> <bch:>     <dbl> <bch:byt> <dbl> <int>
  #> 1 base          48ns  76.8ns    59ns 14.7µs 13013347.        0B     0 10000
  #> 2 before      11.2µs  14.5µs  13.4µs 94.3µs    68865.        0B     3  9997
  #> 3 after        698ns 867.4ns   806ns 24.9µs  1152811.        0B     0 10000
  
  args <- list(foo = missing_arg(), bar = 2)
  bench::mark(
    base = as.call(c(list(as.name("fn")), args)),
    before = call2_before("fn", !!!args),
    after = call2("fn", !!!args)
  )
  #>   expression     min    mean  median     max `itr/sec` mem_alloc  n_gc n_itr
  #>   <bch:expr> <bch:t> <bch:t> <bch:t> <bch:t>     <dbl> <bch:byt> <dbl> <int>
  #> 1 base         777ns  1.02µs   892ns  15.2µs   982750.        0B     0 10000
  #> 2 before        13µs 16.76µs  15.7µs 104.7µs    59670.        0B     2  9998
  #> 3 after        1.4µs  1.74µs   1.6µs  28.5µs   573699.        0B     1  9999
  ```

  Like `pairlist2()`, it preserves empty arguments:

  ```
  call2("[", quote(x), , j = 2)
  #> x[, j = 2]
  ```

* `new_function()` is now implemented in C as well.

title: Refactor dots capture
description:
* Initial steps of dots collection are performed on the captured pairlist. A list is only created when processing splice operators, removing empty arguments, etc. This avoids one alloc and some copies and will make it easier to implement `pairlist2()`.

* Spliced objects are now wrapped in a splice box rather than marked with an attribute. This is cleaner and easier to work with. The splice box always contains a container of the same type. The coercion is parameterised in prevision of `pairlist2()`. 

  These boxes are normally temporary, except wihen capturing dots with `dots_values()`. The latter is useful for processing dots without any copy, which I expect to be important in vctrs since the interface is organised around dots and `!!!`. I plan to use `dots_values()` in `vctrs::vec_type_common()` for instance. A C interface to work with the splice boxes is exposed.

* The splicing step is now completely independent from `flatten()` and `squash()`, which might be removed from the package.

The code is simpler overall, more generic (pairlist2 incoming), and slightly faster.

cc @hadley

title: Export `as_label()`
description:
This is about a replacement for `quo_name()`. I found out that this function is misused by many users for transforming quoted symbols to strings. This is not appropriate because `quo_name()` is a lossy operation and no assumptions should be made about the resulting string. For instance, long symbols might be truncated in the future. The right operator for deterministic symbol-to-string conversion is `as_string()`.

I think the problem stems partly from the function name which suggests it is a getter for "variable names", rather than a lossy transformation. To fix this, the PR introduces a new function `as_label()` to replace `quo_name()`, which I hope will be more suggestive of its purpose. I have also improved the documentation to make it clearer what function to use and when.

This is also relevant to the new naming repair framework for data frames because labellisation is the first step before repairing names because `as_label()` is used internally for automatic naming of captured quosures. This is how unnamed columns in `tibble()` get their names for instance.

I would have liked a greater period of experimentation with this function name but it is likely I will need it for my RStudio conf talk.

Part of #636.

title: Add `as_name()`
description:
* I have reverted the automatic unwrapping of quosures by `as_string()`. This function is now a low-level symbol to string converter.

* The new `as_name()` function is a higher-level variant of `as_string()` which automatically unwraps closures. When rlang gains name-repairing features, `as_name()` should probably get a `syntactic` parameter.

Tidy eval users thus have the choice between `as_label()` to _represent_ an object as a short description, and `as_name()` to _refer_ to an object by its name.

title: Add entrace()
description:
* Add `classes` parameter to `with_abort()`, similar to the new parameter in `catch_cnd()`. Closes #702.

* Rename `add_backtrace()` to `entrace()`. It now supports conditions as well, and so can be used both as a calling handler and as an `options(error = )` handler. `entrace()` now powers `with_abort()`. Closes #699.

* `entrace()` takes `top` and `bottom` arguments, passed to `trace_back()`. By default, it uses an improved detection mechanism for `bottom`. In particular, warnings promoted to errors should now properly be captured.

title: Update lifecycle API
description:
* Move lifecycle badge generation and deprecation signallers in a self-contained `compat-lifecycle.R` file. Draft documentation. I haven't exported these functions yet so we can keep experimenting without constraints. To use this file, packages need rlang in their DESCRIPTION Imports but they don't need to import rlang.

* Change verbosity strategy. Instead of checking the package of the retired function is attached, we now check that the caller of the retired function inherits from the package being tested. The idea is that only people who can do something about the retired function should get a warning (the end user if called from the global env, or the package developer if called during tests).

  To implement this, I check the `TESTTHAT_PKG` environment variable. It isn't set with `devtools::test()` yet but there is an issue opened at https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/issues/787.

* The options have been reviewed. `lifecycle_disable_warnings` disables retirement warnings and `lifecycle_verbose_soft_deprecation` causes soft-deprecated functions to be treated like deprecated functions. A new option `lifecycle_repeat_warnings` causes repeated deprecation warnings instead of once per session.

  To ensure warnings in all cases, we need these three options:

  ```r
  with_options(
    lifecycle_disable_warnings = FALSE,
    lifecycle_verbose_soft_deprecation = TRUE,
    lifecycle_repeat_warnings = TRUE,
    ...
  )
  ```

  ~We could add a `lifecycle_force_warnings` option to set all three above, but it would be a bit confusing to have both this option and `lifecycle_disable_warnings`. It's probably better to add wrappers around `with_options()` etc instead, to get this effect.~

  Added helpers `scoped_lifecycle_warnings()` and `with_lifecycle_warnings()` to force warnings.

title: Add namespace prefixes to backtrace calls
description:
* Exported functions are prefixed with `::`

* Unexported functions are prefixed with `:::`

* Functions inheriting from the global env are prefixed with `global::`.

* Namespace is determined with the topenv rather than the parent env. This way we handle private closures such as `base:::tryCatchOne()`.

```r
library("dplyr")

myfunction <- function() {
  mtcars %>%
    group_by(cyl) %>%
    select(last_col(Inf))
}

myfunction()
#> Error: `offset` must be smaller than the number of columns
#> Call `rlang::last_error()` to see a backtrace

rlang::last_error()
#> <error>
#> * Message: "`offset` must be smaller than the number of columns"
#> * Class: `rlang_error`
#> * Backtrace:
#>  ─global::myfunction()
#>  ─tidyselect::last_col(Inf)
#> Call `summary(rlang::last_error())` to see the full backtrace

summary(rlang::last_error())
#> <error>
#> * Message: "`offset` must be smaller than the number of columns"
#> * Class: `rlang_error`
#> * Fields: `message`, `trace` and `parent`
#> * Backtrace:
#> █
#> ├─global::myfunction()
#> │ └─mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% select(last_col(Inf))
#> │   ├─base::withVisible(eval(quote(`_fseq`(`_lhs`)), env, env))
#> │   └─base::eval(quote(`_fseq`(`_lhs`)), env, env)
#> │     └─base::eval(quote(`_fseq`(`_lhs`)), env, env)
#> │       └─global::`_fseq`(`_lhs`)
#> │         └─magrittr::freduce(value, `_function_list`)
#> │           ├─base::withVisible(function_list[[k]](value))
#> │           └─function_list[[k]](value)
#> │             ├─dplyr::select(., last_col(Inf))
#> │             └─dplyr:::select.grouped_df(., last_col(Inf)) /Users/lionel/Dropbox/Projects/R/hadley/dplyr/R/manip.r:513:2
#> │               └─dplyr:::.select_grouped_df(.data, !!!quos(...), notify = TRUE) /Users/lionel/Dropbox/Projects/R/hadley/dplyr/R/grouped-df.r:212:2
#> │                 └─tidyselect::vars_select(names(.data), !!!quos(...)) /Users/lionel/Dropbox/Projects/R/hadley/dplyr/R/grouped-df.r:205:2
#> │                   └─tidyselect:::vars_select_eval(.vars, quos)

#> │                       └─purrr::map(.x[sel], .f, ...)
#> │                         └─rlang:::.f(.x[[i]], ...)
#> └─tidyselect::last_col(Inf)
```

I added an unexported version of `call_print_type()` that provides a more rigorous breakdowns of calls. I'm still bothered by the current enum returned by `call_print_type()`. Should we unexport it for the time being? Alternatively, it could take a `type = "coarse"` argument that could be set to `"fine"` or `"strict"`.

title: Implement zap sentinel for removing elements
description:
Creating zap objects:

```r
zap()
#> <zap>

zaps(3)
#> [[1]]
#> <zap>
#>
#> [[2]]
#> <zap>
#>
#> [[3]]
#> <zap>

zaps(c("foo", "bar"))
#> $foo
#> <zap>
#>
#> $bar
#> <zap>
```

Zapping arguments:

```r
call <- quote(foo())

call <- call_modify(call, bar = NULL, baz = )
call
#> foo(bar = NULL, baz = )

call_modify(call, bar = zap())
#> foo(baz = )

call_modify(call, !!!zaps(c("foo", "bar", "baz")))
#> foo()
```

Zapping bindings:

```r
env <- env()

env_bind(env, foo = )
env$foo
#>

env_bind(env, foo = NULL)
env$foo
#> NULL

env_has(env, "foo")
#>  foo
#> TRUE

env_bind(env, foo = zap())
env$foo
#> NULL

env_has(env, "foo")
#>   foo
#> FALSE
```

title: Fix !!! input types
description:
Closes #572

Changes for `list2()`:

* Accept pairlists
* Fail with language objects
* Call `base::as.list()` for classed vector objects

Changes for `exprs()` and `quos()`:

* Non-vector non-language objects like environments and functions now fail. Before they were automatically wrapped in a list to allow splicing.

* Call `base::as.list()` for classed vector objects.

* Soft-deprecate splicing of language objects, including scalar quosures. This makes this kind of code throw an error: https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/commit/82ef03af587b5ad57e6edf185a0ca5af8c969d4b#diff-65e6a5a29a28bb3768b7a3c192f952f1R147.

    ```r
    #> Warning message:
    #> Unquoting language objects with `!!!` is soft-deprecated as of rlang 0.3.0.
    #> Please use `!!` instead.
    #>
    #>   # Bad:
    #>   dplyr::select(data, !!!enquo(x))
    #>
    #>   # Good:
    #>   dplyr::select(data, !!enquo(x))    # Unquote single quosure
    #>   dplyr::select(data, !!!enquos(x))  # Splice list of quosures
    #>
    #> This warning is displayed once per session.
    ```

    The soft-deprecation won't be very verbose because there's no reliable way of detecting the caller env, so the warning only occurs when rlang is attached. However we can't deprecate right away because of the tidyr bug (dplyr and tidyselect are fine).

With these changes, and once splicing scalar language objects is defunct, the semantics of `!!!` for `list2()` and `exprs()`/`quos()` will be very similar. I think it'd be a good idea to make them identical. This involves supporting quoted `{` calls in `list2()`:

```r
list2(!!!quote({ foo; bar; }))
#> [[1]]
#> foo
#>
#> [[2]]
#> bar
```

Should we make this change?

title: Add `.check_assign` argument to dots collectors

`list2()` and functions collecting dots with `enquos()` and `enexprs()` now warn when `<-` is passed as argument:

```r
list2(a <- 1)

#>Do you need to use `=` to match an argument?
#>
#>If you really want to use `<-`, please wrap in parentheses:
#>
#>  # Bad:
#>  fn(a <- 1)
#>
#>  # Good:
#>  fn(a = 1)     # Match 1 to parameter `a`
#>  fn((a <- 1))  # Assign 1 to variable `a`
#>[[1]]
#>[1] 1
```

`exprs()` and `quos()` do not warn.

The behaviour is hardcoded for `list2()`, `exprs()` and `quos()`, but can be configured in `dots_list()`, `enexprs()` and `enquos()`.

title: Hook environment for lookups
description:
Includes #152 

- Implements a hook environment as an object table. Requires some trickery to instantiate an environment and set the hashtable to the object table. This environment signals a typed condition when it gets requests for an object.

- Instruments tidyeval overscopes with the hook environment so we get conditions for lookup failures. The hook environment is installed at the end of the lexical scope.


Not as successful as I'd hoped:

- As we discussed grabbing a function is not a distinct operation on object tables, so we can't signal different conditions for symbol lookup and function lookup.

- R often does not call the `exists()` method but uses `get()` and checks for `R_UnboundValue`. In particular it does this when looking up for S3 methods. This means we signal a lot of false positive conditions :(

title: Replace promise-operators with self-evaluating formulas
description:
Includes #16 and #17.

with this patch instead of:

```r
foo <- "bar"
var1 <- ~foo
var2 <- local({ foo <- "baz"; ~foo })
f_quote(list(!!var1, !!var2))
#> ~list(foo, `_P`(~foo))
```

we have:

```r
f_quote(list(!!var1, !!var2))
#> ~list(foo, ~foo)
```

This should make things much more readable when debugging capturing code. The formulas self-evaluate within `f_eval()`:

```r
f_eval(f)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "bar"
#>
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "baz"
```

title: Feature redispatch

Includes #11 

Relevant commit: https://github.com/hadley/rlang/commit/487bd6c536dd890f404a76822613580113c9a42a

I tested redispatch performance with purrr by splitting `as_function()` into two generics, one for mapping and one for indexing. The following `map_()` has a 3ms redispatch cost compared to the original `map()`:

```r
map_ <- function(.x, .f, ...) {
  .f <- rlang::with_redispatch(as_function = "as_pluck",
    as_function(.f, ...)
  )
  .Call(map_impl, environment(), ".x", ".f", "list")
}
```

For `purrr::partial()` rewrite.

I'm not sure if `node_modify()` should take a list instead of dots. That wouldn't be consistent with other `_modify` functions, but that would make sure it doesn't trip on this puzzling bug in R argument matching:

```r
fn <- function(node, ...) node
fn(pairlist(n = arg_missing()), n = "foo")
#> [1] "foo"
```

That seems to only happen for arguments named `n` and affected a purrr example with `runif()`.

title: Self-evaluating formulas and unquote on capture
description:
- There is now two types of unquoting: raw unquoting and promised unquoting. `expr_quote()` and `interp()` with a function or an expression do raw unquoting, while `f_quote()` and `interp()` with a formula do promised unquoting. Also `arg_capture()` does promised unquoting on capture.

  One-sided formulas are considered to be promises when unquoted. `expr_quote()` will inline the RHS while `f_quote()` inserts the formula as is. The trick is that `~` is given a special definition in the `f_eval()` evaluation environment so that the formula can evaluate itself.


- Two-sided formulas don't self-evaluate and so don't need to be guarded to be treated literally. In case a one-sided formula should be treated literally rather than as a promise, it should be unquoted with `UQF()`. This operator changes the call name of the formula from `~` to `_F()`, and `_F()` is defined in the `f_eval()` env to restore the name to `~`.

- `interp()` handles formulas containing unquote operators. It doesn't visit inner formulas so there is actually no need for a "visited" attribute. This is why fpromises are no longer inlined when their environment is not informative, and are unquoted as is instead. Also the consistent unquoting should make it more predictable to new users of tidyeval, as they won't have to learn why the fpromise inlines in some cases but not others.

- `f_eval()` is now more general and can deal with arbitrary expressions. This makes it possible to evaluate a raw expression with pronouns. While probably not very useful, this reflects the fact that tidyeval can deal with raw expressions.

The documentation has been updated to reflect these changes. I think tidy evaluation is now rather complete. A second PR with some file reorganisation and small changes is upcoming (I splitted in two PRs for readability). Now that `f_eval()` is more general, it should probably be an unprefixed verb just like `interp()`. `evaluate()` seems to be a good fit. Or maybe `tidyeval()`?

title: Treat formulas literally and remove UQF()
description:
Closes #74 

With this change, bare formulas are always treated literally.

Now that quosures and bare formulas are treated quite differently, I've changed the quosure print method to make it explicit that an object is a quosure.

```r
quo(foo)
#> # A quosure from the global environment
#> ~foo

new_quosure(quote(foo), base_env())
#> # A quosure from the base environment
#> ~foo

locally(quo(foo))
#> # A quosure from a local environment (0x7fa2e0faf400)
#> ~foo

fn <- function() print(quo(foo))
fn()
#> # A quosure from a frame environment (0x7fa2ea323ed8)
#> ~foo
```

title: Add `.ignore_empty` arg to dots_list() and dots_splice()
description:
So all functions taking dots by value now trim trailing empty arguments by default. E.g.

```r
chr("a", )
#> [1] "a"
```

title: Implement arg_match()
description:
- Doesn't partial match
- Pretty error messages

title: Update splice
description:
This generalises the splicing code to handle flattening (1 level) and squashing (all levels) of lists. Compared to purrr's flatten functions, they have better handling of names:

```r
purrr::flatten_dbl(list(a = 1))
#> [1] 1

rlang::flatten_dbl(list(a = 1))
#> a 
#> 1 
```

And the typed flatten actually do flatten. In purrr they are merely `list_to_type()` coercers:

```r
purrr::flatten_dbl(list(a = 1, list(b = 2)))
#> Error: Can't coerce element 2 from a list to a double

rlang::flatten_dbl(list(a = 1, list(b = 2)))
#> a b 
#> 1 2 
```

Splicing, flattening and squashing have the same handling of names. They all provide an error message if they see a conflict between outer and inner names:

```r
purrr::flatten_dbl(list(a = c(A = 1)))
#> A 
#> 1 

rlang::flatten_dbl(list(a = c(A = 1)))
#> A 
#> 1 
#> Warning message:
#> Outer names are only allowed for unnamed scalar atomic inputs 
```


Also, this introduces `flatten_if()` and `squash_if()` which take a predicate. This predicate can be a closure, a pointer object, or a native info object.

Finally, the `!!!` operator now uses value-based splicing instead of call-based for dots passed by value.

title: Formulas and quosures
description:
##### Handling of quosures

- expr predicates no longer take the RHS of formulas and quosures.

- `type_of()` returns formula for both quosures and formulas. It seems to make more sense to treat all formulas as a base type rather than just quosures.


##### Formula predicates

- the predicates for formulas, quosures and definitions are now more consistent. `is_quosureish()` returns TRUE for quosures and one-sided formula. `is_formulaish()` returns TRUE for definitions and formulas (it is the most general predicate of the family).

- `is_formula()` and `is_formulaish()` gain an `lhs` argument to pattern-match on the presence or absence of LHS.

- `is_formula()` returns TRUE for quosures, but the new `is_bare_formula()` predicate doesn't.


##### Removed functions

- `as_generic_expr()`, `eval_tidy_lhs()`, `eval_tidy_rhs()`

- `as_symbol()`. Its main purpose was to take the CAR of a call if it is a symbol, but it doesn't seem to be an intuitive way of doing this.

- `as_lang()`. It was used to transform symbols to a call, but it seems better to use `lang()` for that purpose. It also used to parse strings into calls, which we now advise against.


##### Pattern-match on namespace in is_lang()

`as_symbol()` was used as part of a suboptimal scheme for handling namespaces in `is_lang()`. This has been replaced by a `ns` argument that allows pattern-matching on namespaces. If `NULL` (the default), the namespace doesn't participate in the match and so `is_lang(quote(foo::bar()), "bar")` and `is_lang(quote(bar()), "bar")` are now equivalent.

title: Fix tidyeval formulas
description:
- Formulas and quosures are now treated separately in tidyeval. Only the latter self-evaluate. Formulas are evaluated (as formulas) in the overscope (more precisely, the parent of the bottom layer since the bottom contains tidyeval definitions for `~` etc).

- Improve genericity of exprs, envs, and quosures a bit.

- Better print method for quosures: `<quosure: local>`. I think the local vs global qualifiers are a bit confusing. How about printing "local" if it's a quosure from the current environment, "frame" if it's a quosure from a frame on the stack, and something else when it's a quosure from outside the current stack? Maybe "external".

title: Use friendly type in error messages
description:
@hadley this currently treats vectors and calls specially:

- vectors are suffixed with "vector", e.g. "an integer vector"
- language are suffixed with "call", e.g. "a language call"

Is this missing anything else?


Also, do we need our own `arg_match()` to get consistent error messages for matched arguments?

title: Fix lazy compat
description:
Includes #88 

This should complete the set of lazy compat methods.

title: Fix symbolic splice
description: Closes #80

title: Tweaks for tidyeval performance
description: Part of https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/2557

title: Update lang API and introduce switchlang()
description:
~~Includes #41~~

* Renames call_ functions to lang_ so we respect the typeof types.

* Rename `lang_standardise()` to `lang_homogenise()` to reflect the fact that it's usually not the function a user is looking for (slow and rarely needed features).

* New faster version `lang_standardise()` which uses `call.match()`.

* Argument matching is now optional in `call_modify()`. This makes it easier to deal with new calls that don't necessarily have a closure defined.

* All these functions have better handling of tidy quotes.

* Adds `lang_head()` and `lang_tail()` for extracting components of a call.

* Introduce `switchlang()` to dispatch on call subtype. The categories are now: `named`, `namespaced`, `inlined` and `recursive`. An error is issued when something other than a function is inlined. This little function already proved quite handy.

title: Support most primitive operators in as_closure()
description:
Closes #75 

Closurised operators have now arguments `.x`, `.y` etc like lambdas created with formulas. This should make it easier to pass arguments, e.g. 

```r
map_int(1:3, `-`, .x = 10)
#> [1] 9 8 7

map_int(1:3, `-` .y = 10)
#> [1] -9 -8 -7
```

title: Fix remaining issues with dictionary class
description:
- Rename `data_source()` to `as_dictionary()`. `is_dictionarish()` is now the predicate for testing uniquely named vectors or environments, and `is_dictionary()` tests for dictionary S3 class.

- Provide replacement methods. The dictionary ctors and coercers have a `read_only` argument to allow replacement. Tidyeval `.data` pronoun is set to read only. `.env` is left as a pure environment because its purpose is now technical, end users should use `!!` to evaluate in the current env.

- Provide a callable entry point for dictionary ctor.

- Export and document the `.data` pronoun.

- Improve the pronoun print method. I didn't put too much effort into it because these pronouns are not typically used interactively.

cc @krlmlr

title: Fix forced dots
description:
This fixes some revdep failures in dplyr due to forced dots being passed to `bind_rows()`. E.g. in this situation:

```r
lapply(x, bind_rows)
```

Forced dots are returned as is when passed by value, and keep issuing an error if passed by expression.

title: Fix dplyr issues
description:
Capturing quosures now:

- has support for missing arguments by returning an empty quosure
- doesn't rewrap quosured literals on repeated captures

This helps simplifying some code in dplyr. It is also more efficient to avoid rewrapping literals (fewer quosure self-evaluation), and I wonder if we should also avoid rewrapping quosures?

In addition, there's now support in `quos()` for removing all empty arguments, none of them, or only trailing ones (the default). This fixes https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/1039

title: Fix formula self eval
description:
* This guards formulas on capture so we are compatible with purrr's lambdas cc @jennybc.

* This streamlines capture of literals so they are not rewrapped in a quosure. This should make it easier for instance to pass default `NULL` arguments between multiple NSE functions and check for a `NULL` quosure.

title: Update expr API and introduce switchpatch()
description:
* Renames `is_lang()` to `is_expr()` and refactors it so it's the union of `is_parsable_literal()` and `is_symbolic()`. Updated documentation reflects the new distinctions.

* Also renames `as_name()` to `as_symbol()`, so we respect the `typeof()` nomenclature.

* Adds `as_name()` which extracts the name of named calls. So now a name is always a string which is consistent with the names attribute.

* Adds `switchpatch()` and `type_of()` for clearer dispatching on base types.

title: New names for quosure functions + S3 quosure class
description:
No class for quosure lists yet.

Also:

- `with_attributes()` is now `struct()` and `zap_attributes()` is `unstruct()`
- `env_set()` renamed to `set_env()`. If called without argument, sets the current env.

title: Implement C backend for splicing
description:
- This adds a number of base-type constructors with splicing semantics. Coercion is currently handled with an R callback to rlang's atomic coercers.

- `dots_list()` and `dots_splice()` are aliases to `splice()` that provide a place to document the two different splicing semantics of `...`.

title: WIP: Splicing and a C++ish API
description:
I thought I'd start working on the R wrapper API while implementing the backend for splicing. It uses a subset of C++:

- Templates and overloading for genericity and propagating type information
- Namespaces to organise code
- POD-only so no dtors issues during long jumps
- Export to R is accomplished by writing a switchpatch function with a pure C signature

title: Add quosure labelling
description:
`quo_expr()` splices all quosures in an expression, and `quo_label()` and `quo_text()` return the label of spliced quosures.

This ensures that anonymous expressions supplied e.g. in dplyr are correctly named.

title: Export and document all pairlist helpers
description: They are useful to manipulate expression trees. E.g. I use them in dplyr to replace some uses of `lazyeval::interp()`.

title: Add functions to deal with character, string, and encoding
description:
`symbol()` and `symbols()` allow symbols to be used within the tidyeval framework without losing the encoding information of strings. They always convert their inputs to the native encoding. This will allow e.g.

```r
select(data, !!! symbols(colnames))
```
cc @krlmlr 

I've added a few functions to help create strings and character vectors with specific encodings. They should make tests easier to write and read. The string functions are mostly equal to the chr_ versions, but check for scalar input.

```r
cafe <- string(c(0x63, 0x61, 0x66, 0xE9), "latin1")
str_bytes(cafe)
str_encoding(cafe)
```

I've documented how locales and encodings are dealt with in R in two places: `str_set_encoding()` discusses why it's important to consistently mark the encoding of strings, and `set_utf8_locale()` discusses the side effects of the `LC_CTYPE` locale.

title: Switch back to promise-climbing
description: Unlike lazyeval, only climb forwarded dots, not symbols.

title: Replace is_numeric() with is_integerish()
description:
- Remove `is_numeric()` as it is a confusing predicate (tests for types instead of concept). Keep `is_bare_numeric()` for testing for base numeric types

- Add `is_integerish()` to check whether a double is close enough to an integer, according to R tolerance rules. Useful when a UI function expects an integer input

title: Remove stack-climbing functions
description: `lang_homogenise()`, `arg_inspect()` and `dots_inspect()` were used for stack climbing but are no longer in use.

title: Tweaks to as_function()
description:
- Handle strings in `as_function()` and `as_closure()`
- Turn `as_function()` to a switchpatch
- Cleaner separation between `as_function()` and `as_closure()`. The former never converts to closures.

title: Another iteration over API naming
description:
- Rename `env()` to `get_env()`, and add new `env()` constructor that creates a new child of the current environment and takes its data as dots (with splicing semantics).

- Unabbreviate `new_` ctors, e.g. `new_fn()` is now `new_function()`. Also `lang()` is now `new_language()`

- `tidy_quote()` and `tidy_quote_expr()` have been renamed to `quosure()` and `expr()`. The previous definition of `quosure()` is now `new_quosure()`.

- `tidy_capture()` and `tidy_quotes()` have been renamed to `arg_quosure()` and `dots_quosures()`. I hope this makes it clearer where the quosures are coming from. E.g. `quosure()` is about the data (code) you supply as input, while `arg_quosure()` is about the data supplied to the argument. `tidy_defs()` is now `dots_definitions()`.

- `parse_f()` and `parse_fs()` are now `parse_quosure()` and `parse_quosures()`.

The plan for documenting the tidyeval functions is to have central documentation about quasiquotation in one place. Then `quosure()`, `expr()`, `arg_quosure()`, `dots_quosures()` and `dots_exprs()` would mention that they support unquoting and link to that page.

title: Coercion functions and NA predicates
description:
- Coercion functions for vectors. They consistently zap attributes except names, they bypass base S3 methods, and avoid copying atomic vectors when not needed.

- NA predicates. The `is_` variants are scalar, and `are_` variants are vectorised.

- Environment functions: turn generic `env()` to a switchpatch and rename `new_env()` to `child_env()`, since new_ is for S3 stuff.

title: Tidy capture of dots
description:
Includes #22, #23, #24 and #25

The `:=` operator is now called the pattern operator, with predicate function `is_pattern()`.

`tidy_dots()`:

- now interpolates on capture.
- accepts splice-unquote in dots: `tidy_dots(foo, !!! captured_dots)`
- evaluates the LHS of patterns (formulas of type `a := b`) and treats it as dot name, unless `patterned = FALSE`. If another name is supplied with a pattern (e.g. `var = a := b`, throws a warning).


`tidy_patterns()`:

- Returns patterns as is, with both LHS and RHS interpolated.
- Accepts names: `tidy_patterns(pat = a := b)`.

title: Compatibility with R 3.1.0
description:
Includes #22, #23 and #24 

3.1.0 is not yet enabled on Travis because of a bug in devtools (and it's hard to install the dev version on R 3.1 because it lacks `https` support in download functions).

title: Add quosure predicates for expressions
description: To replace expression predicates as they no longer take the RHS.

title: Fix environment supplied as data to eval_tidy()
description: Closes #104

title: Improve set_attrs()
description:
- `set_attrs()` now fails with uncopyable objects
- `mut_attrs()` can be used to explicitly change attributes with side effects
- if called with unnamed `NULL`, zap attributes

Also, `_len()` and `_along()` ctors don't pass `...` to `set_attrs()` anymore. It doesn't seem as readable as an explicit call to `set_attrs()`.

title: Improve deparsing of expressions
description:
- Adds `warn` argument to `quo_expr()`. This will be useful for porting dtplyr to tidyeval because we'll need to flatten quosures.

- Split `quos_auto_name()` from `exprs_auto_name()`. The latter gains a `printer` argument that will help with https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/2686

title: Polish API and documentation for lang and expr functions
Update of env API and doc
description:
- merge `env_assign()`, `env_bind()` and `env_define()` in one function `env_bind()` that takes dots with splicing syntax

- rename `env_assign_promise()` and `env_assign_active()` to `env_bind_exprs()` and `env_bind_fns()`. They now take dots. The former takes dots with `exprs()` and supports unquoting.

- `env_bury()` now takes dots as well.

- Refactoring of documentation.

title: Implement seq2() and seq2_along()
description:
Closes #76 

Do you prefer `seq_inc()` instead of `seq2()`? But then I'm not sure how to call `seq2_along()`.

title: Import new set_names() features from purrr
description:
Also:

- fix `set_names(x, NULL)`
- pass names to `chr()` to gain splicing semantics
- pass `...` to `nm` when it's a function

This exports `dots_n()` though I ended up removing it from `set_names()` implementation.

title: Fix partial matching in env_bind()
description: And rename `parent` argument to `.parent` in `child_env()`.

title: Fix symbol collision with tidyr::replace_na()
description: Closes #133

title: Evaluate tilde calls in overscope
description: Fixes https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/2745

title: Fix capture of optimised promises
description:
This fixes the "Argument was already evaluated" error of the lisy and epidata packages.

This one is kind of serious. Should we make another rlang release before dplyr's?

cc @krlmlr

title: Implement env_set()
description:
Closes #162 

This probably all should be rewritten in C to avoid performance issues when rlang functions are used in loops (e.g. #151).

* Should we go with a separate `scope_set()` function that would have a different default value for `create`?

* Should `env_bind()` and variants gain a `.create` argument as well?

title: Expand C API
description:
This moves quosure self-evaluation and several functions to C.

I'm experimenting with new principles for the UI:

- All allocators like `r_pairlist()` or `r_new_language()` protect their arguments. Underscored versions do not protect. This is intended to make it easier to create data structures, e.g. no need to protect a transient newly allocated string before assigning it in a container. This convention is only for allocators, other functions expect protected arguments.

- PROTECT and UNPROTECT are aliased to the shorter KEEP and FREE to declutter code.

title: Informative error message when coercing a ctrl flow primitive
description:
Closes #158 

Also improve doc about the formals names returned for primitives.

title: enquo() as alias to quo() when called at top-level
description: ~~lncludes a review of the call stack UI as I got confused by a simple `call_depth()` (even though I ended up using `sys.parent()` to make the top-level check).~~ This is now in #197

title: Parse unicode points when call-splicing a list
description: Part of tidyverse/dplyr#2886

title: Fix couple of bugs before release
description:
- `eval_tidy()` does not map over lists anymore.
- `cnd_signal()` accepts character vectors of S3 classes and returns `NULL` invisibly.

title: Fix .env pronoun
description: The `.env` pronoun should refer to the current quosure env. Closes #174.

title: Support for R 3.1
description: Looks like devtools isn't compatible with 3.1 because of `trimws()`. I have added a compat that could be used to fix this.

title: Force package developers to explicitly register experimental functions
description: Simple approach that makes sure depending on an experimental function is intentional.

title: Add experimental support for `.Last.error`
description:
When rlang is loaded `.Last.error` is installed as a delayed binding that offers to enable error capture. If "no" is selected a taskCallback resets the delayed binding (Luke mentioned on r-devel that it might make sense to provide an official way of resetting delayed bindings but that was not implemented yet AFAICT --- Also an active binding wouldn't work here because top-level handlers have to be installed by top-level calls).

```r
.Last.error
#> Would you like to enable `.Last.error` capture?
#>
#> 1: Yes
#> 2: No

#> Selection: 1
#> Capture of uncaught errors in `.Last.error` is now enabled
```

Once enabled, uncaught errors are recorded in `.Last.error`:

```r
.Last.error
#> NULL

stop("bim")
#> Error: bim

.Last.error
#> <simpleError: bim>

f <- function() stop("bam")
f()
#> Error in f(): bam

.Last.error
#> <simpleError in f(): bam>
```

However errors thrown at top-level (from a primitive function) reset the calling handler stack, so users have to restore the stack manually. This requires two steps because we can only add top-level handlers from a top-level call such as triggered by a delayed binding.

```r

data[1]
#> Recording of errors is now disabled, please call `rlang:::enable_last_error()`
#> Error in data[1] : object of type 'closure' is not subsettable

rlang:::enable_last_error()
#> Now type `.Last.error` at the console to enable error recording

.Last.error
#> Capture of uncaught errors in `.Last.error` is now enabled
```

title: Rewrite call_standardise()
description: and add some tools for pairlists.

title: arg introspection
description: Includes #1

title: Fix formal name
description:
This adds a `name` field to `arg_info()`'s output. It reports the name of the original formal argument. This is used in the lazyeval compatibility layer because `lazy()` returns the formal name when the argument is missing (whereas `arg_info()` and `arg_expr()` return the missing arg for consistency).

To make this possible `call_standardise()` gains a `add_missings()` argument so that `f()` is expanded to `f(x = )`. I wonder if `add_missings` and `enum_dots` should be gathered in a single bool argument `full`?

title: Fix Recall()
description:
Includes #3

This patch adds post-processing in `call_stack()` to restore continuity in the stack when `Recall()` is involved. Call arguments and caller positions need to be adjusted.

This is one step in making `arg_info()` compatible with the next version of magrittr in which `freduce()` applies the function sequence recursively with `Recall()`. To make magrittr fully compatible requires two additional upstream changes:

*  Break the chain of passed arguments by renaming `value` to another name before passing it to elements of the function sequence.

*  Pass to these functions an argument called `.` so that

   ```r
   mtcars %>% lazyeval::lazy_dots()
   ```

   returns `lazy$expr` = `.`. For instance `dplyr::do()` relies on this.

E.g.

```{r}
freduce <- function(value, function_list) {
  . <- value
  if (length(function_list) == 1L)
    function_list[[1L]](.)
  else
    Recall(function_list[[1L]](.), function_list[-1L])
}
```

We could make these changes to magrittr, release a new version, and have lazyeval or rlang depend on that magrittr version to make sure we are compatible. cc @smbache


I noticed one more incompatibility in that `mtcars %>% lazy()` returns `.` as lazy expr with the new rlang backend, while it inlines mtcars with the old promise-based backend. But I don't think we can do anything on that front. I'm rerunning the revdep checks, hopefully that won't be an issue.

title: Move type predicates from purrr to rlang
description: I also added a discussion of closures vs primitives in `?is_function`. Maybe that should be a vignette?

title: Environment functions
description:
Includes #6 

On hindsight, maybe whether to look in parent environments should be an argument like in base R. Currently this is being handled in different verbs. E.g. `env_sees()` rather than `env_has(fetch = TRUE)`.

title: Switch to new capture approach
description:
Includes #7 

* Rename `f_capture()` to `arg_capture()`. `arg_capture()` and `dots_capture()` now work only across one call level.
* `arg_expr()`, `arg_label()` work across one call level as well. Remove `arg_env()` since it would be synonymous with `env_caller()` / `parent.frame()`.
* Rename `arg_info()` and `dots_info()` to `arg_inspect()` and `dots_inspect()`. These functions use the call stack for introspection and their limitations are documented.

title: Condition handling
description:
Includes #6 and #7.

Also some functions for non-local returns since they are related to restarts.

title: Moving purrr's general functions to rlang
description:
- This moves the rest of purrr's general-purpose functions to rlang.
- The handler constructors now use `as_function()` to accept lambda-formulas.
- `modify()` as you suggested on Slack. I called it like this to mirror `call_modify()`. Maybe it should be `lst_modify()` or `list_modify()`.
- `with_attributes()` is like `structure()` but accepts a list in addition to dots.
- The `_along()` family handles all vector types and is completed with `_until()` family. Should the latter be `_len()` as in `rep_len()`?

Also the vector constructors accept attributes. Not sure this is a good idea though:

```r
list_along(letters, class = "s3_class")
```

versus:

```r
with_attributes(list_along(letters), class = "s3_class")
```

title: Potpourri of new functions
description:
I particularly like the new implementation of `invoke()`. It creates clean call stacks. Does it make sense to have `invoke()` in rlang, and keep the invoke-map versions in purrr? Maybe it'd be better to rename `.args` to `.x` for cross-package consistency, though `.x` feels more like purrr than rlang.

cc @hadley

title: UI environments
description:
Includes #22 

This PR updates the UI to reflect the prefix = input type and suffix = output type principle.

- Namespace functions have been renamed from `env_namespace()` to `ns_env()`. Named environments like `env_global()` have been renamed to `global_env()`. New `pkg_` and `scoped_` prefixes for functions about package environments and the search path.

- Renamed `as_quoted_f()` to `as_fquote()`. `parse_expr_f()` to `parse_f()` since it returns a formula. And `has_names()` to `has_name()` to reflect that it's vectorised.

- Renamed `dict` argument of env functions to `data`, since that is more in line with other similar arguments like in `tidy_eval()`. The concept of dictionary is still mentioned in the docs and I wonder if the `data_source` class should be renamed to `dictionary`. I think we should formally define the concept of dictionary as part of our reflections on S3 and generic programming and it seems like data sources for tidy evaluation are an instance of that, just like environment is an instance of dictionary (which is why data sources were modelled after environments).

title: UI ctors
description:
Includes #22 and #23.

This simply renames all constructors to use `new` as prefix rather than suffix.

title: Switch to stack-climbing in dots_capture()
description:
To remove last remnants of promise-climbing in the package.

Includes #11.

title: Ui tidyeval
description:
New UI for tidyeval and some fixes:

- `tidy_quote()`, `tidy_interp()`, `tidy_eval()`

- `tidy_eval_lhs()` and `tidy_eval_rhs()` evaluate in place.

- `tidy_quote_expr()` returns an expression. It does not perform "raw unquoting" anymore (automatically taking the RHS). Doing so was making the code complicated and it was harder to document, especially with `tidy_interp()` which would have require a new argument to that effect.

- `tidy_eval_env()` is exported for packages that implement their own tidy evaluation scheme. It is paired with a cleanup function that removes the `~` self-evaluating definitions in case the environment leaks somewhere. For example if the evaluated expression captures the eval env by creating a closure.

- Unquote operators are now inlined during interpolation rather than made available in the interpolation env. This way unquoting has "frame consistent" semantics when the interpolation environment is leaked by creating a formula or closure.


New `expr` functions:

- `arg_label()` etc are renamed to `expr_label()` since they take an expression.

- New `expr_eval()` function for lightweight and "stack consistent" evaluation. It's a simple wrapper around `Rf_eval()` and is a better way than creating and forcing a promise. In the places where it's important to keep the call stack clean, like `invoke()`, `Rf_eval()` can be called directly via `.Call(rlang_eval, expr, env)`.

title: Wrap-up tidyeval
description:
Includes #19.

Reorganisation of files and some other small changes. This is a second PR because of the file renaming noise.

title: Make backtrace display optional
description:
~Includes #608~

* Backtraces are no longer displayed by default.

* Introduces the experimental option `rlang__backtrace_on_error`. It can be set to `reminder` (to remind the user to call `rlang::last_error()` to see a backtrace), `branch`, `collapse` or `full` (to control the verbosity of the backtrace).

    See [test-on-error-message-options.txt](https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/pull/609/files#diff-1b9d45add965cd1603af2dff672624ad) for the different outputs.

The reminder is displayed with `crayon::silver()` as an approximation to `crayon::blurred()` which doesn't work in RStudio. This makes the reminder appear dimmer than the error message. Perhaps the whole backtrace should get this treatment?

In packages, `abort()` can be wrapped like this:

```r
my_abort <- function(...) {
  with_options(
    rlang__backtrace_on_error = "reminder",
    abort(...)
  )
}

my_abort("foo")
#> Error: foo
#> Call `rlang::last_error()` to see a backtrace
```

Is this sufficient or do we still need the extra argument @hadley?

title: Add parentheses to call CAR when printing if required (#581)
description:
Fixes #581 by adding a check to `call_deparse()` to see if the expression in the CAR slot of the call should be wrapped in parentheses for printing.

I picked the expressions that should have parentheses using the switch statement from `op_deparse()` and eyeballing which ops should have parentheses and which not.

title: Remove trace methods
description: They don't respect vector invariants, such as: `length(x)` returns the number of elements you can subset with `[[`. This was causing `str()` to fail.

title: WIP: Use expr_deparse() in deparsing functions
Switch to "mask" in remaining rlang API
description: Following the switch from overscope to data mask, it seems we should also switch from "symbol burrying" to "symbol masking". I've never been happy with the name of `env_bury()` but `env_mask()` feels right.

title: Gracefully handle expr_text(<symbol>).
description:
When the expression is a bare symbol, rather use as_string and its magic handling of encoding. closes #611

Same fix as https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/3830 but potentially benefitting outside of dplyr.

title: Implement str() method for rlang errors
description:
Includes #608.

Compared to the print method which displays a simplified backtrace, `str()` displays the full call tree as well as the condition fields. This makes it easy to print the full backtrace of the last error:

```
str(last_error())
```

See [test-cnd-error-str.txt](https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/pull/610/files#diff-049078f9aaca010092da520fab9d7269) for an example output.

title: Add last_error()
description:
This is an approximation to saving unhandled errors for later retrieval. Ideally we'd use a top-level handler. Since we can't do that, we save the errors when they are printed at the console. This normally only happens when the error goes unhandled.

There are some exceptions, for example a verbose `try()` calls `conditionMessage()`, or errors demoted to warnings in the namespace loading code. That seems alright because in general the conditionMessage method is called when the error message is printed at the console and then it makes sense to provide a means of retrieving it.

cc @gaborcsardi @jimhester

title: Fix typo in eval_tidy() doc
description: typo

title: Update data mask API
description:
* Deprecate bare environments passed to `eval_tidy()` and `as_data_mask()` Passing bare environments is confusing because their parents is silently changed to the current evaluation env. (There is a similar confusion in `base::eval()` except that it goes the other way around, the current evaluation env is silently ignored.)

* Deprecate `parent` arguments of `as_data_mask()` and `new_data_mask()`.

The idea behind these two changes is that the parent of the data mask is undetermined at time of creation. The parent changes during evaluation to the `env` argument of `eval_tidy()`, or to quosure environments when applicable. Given these semantics, allowing parents at data mask creation and supporting bare environments were confusing.

Closes #571

title: Fix handling of indent_status in deparse()
description:
The increase_indent() function was actually creating an invalid
object via the expression `new_node(FALSE, 0L)`.

The `new_node` function is a wrapper for the `cons()` function, which
expects two arguments:

* car: the value of the node to be created
* tail (or cdr): a pairlist (or NULL) which continues the list after the  new node created

The expression `new_node(FALSE, 0L)` then actually passes an integer vector
as the cdr or tail instead of a pairlist, creating an illegal object.

You can verify this by evaluating the following expressions:

     x <- new_node(FALSE, 0L)
     length(x[[1]])

Which will crash your R session.

The code does work at the moment because GNU R does not actually check
that the cdr argument to the cons() function is valid, and the value is
only accessed via the CDR macros, which also do not verify the expression.

Other interpreters (e.g. Renjin) are not so forgiving however.

Implement enquos()
description:
It is awkward to transition from `enquo()` to `quos()` while teaching tidy eval, and users have reported this naming to be confusing. `enquos()` should make things easier. The difference between the two are:

- `enquos()` only takes symbols while `quos()` accepts any expressions.
- supplying symbols to `enquos()` is like using `enquo()` on each of them. I.e. it captures arguments one level up.
- both capture arguments passed to `...` the same way.

```r
capture_quos <- function(foo, ...) quos(foo, ...)
capture_quos(bar, quux)
#> [[1]]
#> <quosure>
#>   expr: ^foo
#>   env:  0x7fdab7ca0238
#>
#> [[2]]
#> <quosure>
#>   expr: ^quux
#>   env:  global

capture_enquos <- function(foo, ...) enquos(foo, ...)
capture_enquos(bar, quux)
#> [[1]]
#> <quosure>
#>   expr: ^bar
#>   env:  global
#>
#> [[2]]
#> <quosure>
#>   expr: ^quux
#>   env:  global
``` 

Closes #323

title: Pretty printer for quosures
description:
After using the flat printing style for a while I think that hiding quosures is actually more confusing. Otoh displaying quosures as formulas is confusing as well because R users don't think of formulas as something that evaluates, e.g. when they see `list(~letters)` they expect to get a list containing `~letters` rather than the letters vector.

So how about printing quosures with a leading `^`? This PR uses a naive approach to printing but it should work fine in most cases until we have a custom expression printer in rlang:

```r
quo(foo)
#> ^foo

local(quo(foo))
#> ^foo
#> <environment: 0x7fc9d305d008>

quo(foo(!!quo(bar())))
#> ^foo(^bar())
```

title: Fix bang bang precedence
description:
This adds a rotating version of interpolation / expansion for operators with problematic precedence. The general expansion + rotation strategy is described in [expr-interp-rotate.c](https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/compare/master...lionel-:fix-bang-bang-precedence?expand=1#diff-52691165fd88c9bb6ace5dc84ed116f0).

I am using [Linux kernel documentation style](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v4.9/kernel-documentation.html#writing-kernel-doc-comments) for embedded documentation. After a quick review of available options it seems like the cleanest syntax. A [perl script](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/scripts/kernel-doc) can be used to generate Sphinx output from the C files. This might be a good option to generate the documentation of the C wrapper library later on.

* [dots.c](https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/compare/master...lionel-:fix-bang-bang-precedence?expand=1#diff-3b4f8126fe47843caf246e738300bee2) / [dots.h](https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/compare/master...lionel-:fix-bang-bang-precedence?expand=1#diff-304617922aa93ebf3b6880ddb65ff217) / [expr-interp.c](https://github.com/lionel-/rlang/blob/cbb6dcba43ebc0b939e9a89dd1f6960041d5bd30/src/expr-interp.c): Add a FIXUP operation type. The expansion + rotation algorithm is only used for problematic operators (binary ops whose precedence is between prec(`!`) and prec(`!!`) to avoid the overhead for the normal unquoting case.

* [parse.c](https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/compare/master...lionel-:fix-bang-bang-precedence?expand=1#diff-984682cffd12ab2ca3a98d41cd829a96) / [parse.h](https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/compare/master...lionel-:fix-bang-bang-precedence?expand=1#diff-fd510818d73257282d4b4b827e37d05b): `r_which_operator()` tokenises a symbol to an `enum r_operator`. The operation precedence table `r_ops_precedence` contains information for programming on the language with operators (binding power, unary, delimited).

* [rlang.h](https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/compare/master...lionel-:fix-bang-bang-precedence?expand=1#diff-50ed1f2855cf86cb0d682acdfecaee1d) / [init.c](https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/compare/master...lionel-:fix-bang-bang-precedence?expand=1#diff-885908120835b66f90958a39baeb2018): Add a static assertion macro borrowed from Linux source code and use it to check that tables (such as operation precedence table) are correctly initialised at compile-time. To work around the limitations of static assertions the elements of the table are checked at load time.

* [expr-interp-rotate.c](https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/compare/master...lionel-:fix-bang-bang-precedence?expand=1#diff-52691165fd88c9bb6ace5dc84ed116f0): Implementation of the expand + rotate algorithm for binary operators with problematic precedence.

* [test-tidy-unquote.R](https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/compare/master...lionel-:fix-bang-bang-precedence?expand=1#diff-20d2c7b15a736c94480c1004c35eab17): Unit tests for the new operator precedence.
  [test-c-api.R](https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/pull/328/files#diff-810e014010775ef58cadc8b13416a131): Unit tests for the `enum r_operator` tokeniser.

description:
* Greatly improves the speed of evaluation when there is no overscope. Closes https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/388.

* Quosures no longer require evaluation within an overscope, which means the original environment can be preserved. Implementation of "safe" quosures that would never be overscoped even when `data` is supplied should now be a few lines patch (see #309).

* `as_overscope()` now takes `data` instead of a quosure which makes more sense. This is a breaking change but I don't see any CRAN package using `as_overscope()`.

* The main downside is that raw quosures don't print nicely now that they are calls to a thunk rather than to the symbol `~`. The quosure print method hides this but users will encounter strange print output if they embed quosures in raw expressions, e.g. `expr(list(!! quo(foo))`.

* Another downside is the printing bug that affects all language objects with a class and causes them to be evaluated during printing if they are wrapped in a list, e.g. `list(quo(foo))`. This doesn't cause issues with formulas but will trigger strange errors with the new quosures. We'll propose a fix to the R printer soon. The `quosures` print method works around it so lists returned by `quos()` are not affected.

* The print method for quosures is now a bit nicer. It appears like a simple expression with the environment displayed beneath.

Includes #297, closes #279.

To treat `expr(list(a := foo))` as synonym of `expr(list(a = foo))` and allow name-unquoting everywhere.

I'm not too fond of the `unquote_names` argument name, but I can't think of anything better.

title: Remove one layer of parentheses around !!
description:
Includes #297 and #301.

With this change `(!! sym("foo"))(arg)` expands to `foo(arg)` instead of `(foo)(arg)`. It is possible to double wrap to force the parentheses: `((!! 1)) + 1` expands to `(1) + 1`.

title: Implement dots capture in C
description:
Closes #201, #217, #242, #267, #280, #290, #295

The bulk of the refactor is in https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/pull/297/files#diff-3b4f8126fe47843caf246e738300bee2:

`dots_unquote()` walks the captured dots, evaluates the unquoted expressions and records the size of spliced values. It ignores empty argument depending on the value of `ignore_empty`. A switchpatch ensures the dots values are correctly wrapped depending on the target type (raw expressions, quosures, values). A second function `dots_interp()` is in charge of building the final list.

The new implementation puts dots capture with few arguments on the order of 3 to 10 µs, a bit more if splicing is involved (mostly because a larger final vector is allocated and filled). With the previous implementation it was often on the order of milliseconds.

On my machine the following expression takes 50 ms with CRAN rlang but 45 µs with this PR:

```r
quos(
  foo, bar(), foo,
  !!! letters,
  !! letters[[4]] := foo,
  !!! letters,
  !! letters[[4]] := foo,
  !!! letters,
  !! letters[[4]] := foo
)
```

The dots capture functions have a more consistent interface (e.g. `exprs()` accepts `.named` argument). Also they now all accept forced arguments, which are treated as if they were unquoted.

Unquoting has been improved which also benefits `enquo()` and `enexpr()`. Unquoting is now faster with `expr()` than with `bquote()`.

title: Fix bang bang operator precedence
description:
This fixes the parse tree so that `!!` binds tightly:

```r
foo <- "foo"

expr(!! foo * bar == baz)
#> "foo" * bar == baz

expr(!! foo %>% bar())
#> "foo" %>% bar()
```

Change predicates so that:

- "pairlist node" refers to pairlist type, i.e. a cons cell.

This definition hasn't changed:

- "pairlist" refers to both pairlist and NULL types. This is consistent with lisp where `nil` is the empty list.

title: Fix symbol encoding
description:
Includes #34 

Relevant commit: https://github.com/hadley/rlang/commit/8736dc5d3164bba881c43855d81ae1fc7793006d

With this version of `symbol()`, UTF-8 tagged strings are properly store in new symbols. The drawback is that if a symbol has been created beforehand with `as.name()`, the untagged string is cached in the symbol table and there is nothing `symbol()` can do anymore. Hopefully this doesn't cause too much problems, since users are more likely to create strings than symbols, and we'd advise to always use `symbol()` or `as_name()`.

title: Add a Makevars file for unity builds
description:
This forces 'rlang.c' to be recompiled if any of it's dependencies are out
of date.

Rather than requiring pkgbuild modifications an easier solution might be to use a Makevars which handles the dependency resolution.

Taking this idea further could have `rlang.c` written based on the `files` variable in the Makevars, which would remove the redundant filenames. You could also populate `files` with wildcards so they wouldn't have to be listed explicitly, but this requires GNU make extensions.

Fixes https://github.com/r-lib/pkgload/issues/50, https://github.com/r-lib/pkgbuild/pull/13

title: C API for signaling conditions
description:
Because R's C API does not have a direct way to signal a condition, this
implementation simply constructs a condition object and calls the R
`signalCondition` function.

This file is located in `inst/include` so that other packages can use it
by adding `LinkingTo: rlang` to their DESCRIPTION. The function is
static so it will be copied to each compilation unit, avoiding multiple
definition errors. `inline` is not part of the c89 standard, so cannot
be used without `-std=c99` or compiler extensions.

This API assumes the condition object will contain only only one (additional) class and no additional values apart from the message, we can discuss if we should provide a more flexible API or if this is sufficient. I am also not sure if we need to expose the evaluation env, or if always evaluating the  `signalCondition()` call in the global environment is sufficient.
